title: Getting Your First Customer
subtitle: Move from “I have a business” to “someone paid me,” the small but important plot twist

blocks.text: Your first customer probably will not arrive because your new logo sensed a disturbance in the economy. Logos are talented, but they rarely make phone calls. A first sale usually comes from one clear offer, one suitable person and one useful conversation.

The goal is not to convince everyone. It is to find one person with a real problem you can solve safely and at a profit, then make the next step easy. Your early process can be simple: pick a narrow customer, build a short list of people to contact, ask questions, send a written offer, follow up and deliver exactly what you promised.
Your first customer is proof, not a lifetime business plan. Use the sale to learn who buys, why they buy, what delivery costs you and what to improve.

items.title: “I need a large audience before I can make a sale.”
items.text: One useful conversation can matter more than 2,000 followers who do not care. Your first customer needs a reason to act, not a stadium.

blocks.text: Canada: Planning a business
Landing one paying customer proves your idea works and shows you how to find the next one.
blocks.detail: A clear offer, a short list of the right people and one good conversation do more than a polished logo.
blocks.extra: Section 02 helps you write an offer people understand in one sentence.

sections.title: Make It Easy to Understand and Easy to Buy

blocks.text: Describe your offer in one sentence: “I help [a specific customer] solve [a specific problem] by providing [a defined service or product] for [a price or starting price].”

items.title: CHOOSE THE CUSTOMER
items.text: Start with one group whose problem, budget and way of buying you understand. “Local landlords with one to five units” gives clearer direction than “anyone who owns walls.”

items.title: NAME THE RESULT
items.text: Describe the useful result, not every task. A customer buys a clean move-out inspection, a working booking page or three ready freezer meals, not your internal checklist.

items.title: SET A STARTER SCOPE
items.text: Limit the time, place, number of revisions, materials, delivery and what is left out. A small, fixed, paid trial can lower the risk for both of you without turning free work into “exposure.”

items.title: PRICE THE WHOLE JOB
items.text: Include preparation, travel, materials, fees, messages, delivery, tax and follow-up. Say your deposit, when payment is due and your cancellation terms before work starts.

blocks.text: Market research starts with what customers and competitors tell you. Ten short conversations can show you the words, worries and reasons to buy that a month of logo polishing never will.
A paid trial should have a real scope and a fair price. A discount can support a test. Underpricing for good teaches customers a lesson you did not intend.

items.title: “The lowest price wins the first customer.”
items.text: Price is only one reason people choose. Being relevant, trusted, proven, fast, clear and low-risk can matter more than being the cheapest stranger.

sections.title: Invite a Next Step, Not a Parade

blocks.text: Build a list of 20 people who are likely to fit, from your own network, local groups, referrals, public business directories or suitable community groups. Note why each one may fit.

items.title: Warm introduction
items.text: Tell people you trust exactly who you help, and ask whether one suitable introduction comes to mind. Do not ask them to “send anyone with money.”

items.title: Outreach with permission
items.text: Use each channel properly and follow Canada’s Anti-Spam Legislation. Promotional emails and texts generally need consent, your name and contact details, and a working way to unsubscribe.

items.title: Discovery conversation
items.text: Ask what is happening now, what result matters, what they have tried, their timing, who decides and what budget feels comfortable. Listen before you pitch.

items.title: Written next step
items.text: Sum up the problem, the result, the scope, the price, the timing, who does what and how they say yes. Give a deadline only if it is real.

blocks.text: A good first message is short: something relevant you noticed, a specific result, one reason you can help and a low-pressure question. Personal means relevant, not pasting a first name into a novel.
Follow up once or twice with something new or a clear yes-or-no question. Silence is information. It is not permission to begin a 14-message documentary series.

items.title: “A good salesperson handles every objection immediately.”
items.text: An objection may mean missing information, bad timing, the wrong decision-maker, a poor fit or an honest no. Ask one respectful question, answer truthfully and let the customer decide.

blocks.text: Before you deliver, send a short invoice or written confirmation with your business name, the date, what you will do, the price and when payment is due. It looks professional, it settles questions later and it is the first record for your taxes.
Tax basics for your first year

items.title: REPORT IT
items.text: Business income goes on Form T2125 with your personal tax return, whether clients pay by cash, cheque or e-transfer.

items.title: PAY BOTH HALVES OF CPP
items.text: Self-employed people pay the worker and employer shares of CPP, 11.9% of net business income above the basic amount, on Schedule 8 of the return.

items.title: SET MONEY ASIDE
items.text: Nobody takes tax off your pay. Move a share of every payment into a separate account. If you owe more than $3,000 ($1,800 in Quebec) this year and in either of the last two years, the CRA will ask for quarterly instalments.

items.title: KEEP RECORDS SIX YEARS
items.text: Keep invoices, receipts, mileage and bank records for six years from the end of the tax year they belong to.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: your first customer comes from focus and trust. Choose one suitable buyer, understand a real need, make a specific written offer, follow up with respect and deliver what you promised before you chase growth.
Meet Leah
paragraphs: Leah Martin opens a small digital services business in Winnipeg. Her goal is one paying client within a month, to prove to herself this can work. Her first post offers websites, social media, logos, newsletters, videos and “basically anything online.” It is less an offer and more a department store wearing one laptop.
Three weeks pass with no sale. She posts every day, but nobody knows which problem to bring her.
Then she has coffee with Samir, who owns a small physiotherapy clinic. She almost launches into her full menu. Instead, she decides to ask questions and listen.
Samir mentions that new patients keep phoning the front desk because the clinic’s booking page is confusing on a phone. Some give up and never book.

Leah offers a small, paid trial. She will fix that one booking page, test it on a phone and allow one round of changes, all within seven days. She writes down the price, the logins she needs and what is not included. Samir says yes. The result is clear and the risk is small.
She delivers on time. The twist comes a month later. Samir says booking calls are down by half, and he introduces her to two other clinic owners with the same problem.
Leah’s first customer did not buy “everything digital.” He bought one easier path to an appointment, which was considerably simpler to invoice. She rewrites her offer around clinic booking pages.

blocks.text: Ask for feedback after you deliver: what changed, what was easiest, what made them hesitate and who else has the same problem. Ask permission before you share a name, quote or result.
What resolved the conflict?
A narrow, specific offer replaced a vague menu of everything, and gave one person a reason to say yes.
Leah landed her first client, and two referrals, by asking questions and fixing one real problem.
blocks.detail: One clear, paid trial can turn your own first conversation into a steady source of work.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: What belongs in a one-sentence offer?
items.detail: The specific customer, the specific problem, the defined service or product, and the price or starting price.

items.title: Why is a short list of the right people useful?
items.detail: Twenty people with a clear reason to fit is a sales plan. A huge list of strangers is just noise to work through.

items.title: What should happen in a discovery conversation?
items.detail: Ask what is happening now, what result matters, what they have tried, timing, who decides and what budget feels comfortable. Then listen before you pitch.

items.title: Which details belong in a written offer?
items.detail: The problem, the result, the scope, the price, the timing, who does what, how they accept and a deadline only if it is real.

items.title: What does a respectful follow-up avoid?
items.detail: Pressure. One or two follow-ups with something new or a clear yes-or-no question is enough.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): First-Customer Launch Card

blocks.text: Use business contact details only. Do not write passwords, card numbers, sensitive personal details or private notes about people here.

Collect only the customer information you need for a stated reason, get real consent where it is required and keep it safe. Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec also have their own private-sector privacy laws.

items.title: Ideal customer
items.text: The narrow group most likely to need and value your offer.

items.title: Value proposition
items.text: The clear reason a customer should choose your offer.

items.title: Qualified prospect
items.text: A possible customer with a real need, a good fit and the power to decide.

items.title: Discovery conversation
items.text: Questions you ask to understand someone before suggesting a solution.

items.title: Scope
items.text: The written limits of what you will and will not deliver.

items.title: Conversion
items.text: Moving from one sales step to the next, such as from a conversation to a paying customer.

items.title: CASL
items.text: Canada’s Anti-Spam Legislation, which sets consent and ID rules for commercial emails and texts.

quiz.question: True or False: “I need a large audience before I can make a sale.”

questions: Who is your specific customer, and what problem will you solve? Use the one-sentence offer.
What is included in your starter offer, what is left out and what is the price?
Name three people or groups on your list of 20, and why each might fit.
What are three questions you will ask in your first conversation?
How will they say yes, and how will they pay? For example, an email reply and an e-transfer deposit.
When will you follow up, and when will you stop?
samples: I help small clinics fix confusing booking pages so new patients book online, from $450.
One booking page, tested on a phone, one round of changes, done in 7 days. No new website.
A physio clinic I visit, a chiropractor a friend knows, a dental office in my neighbourhood.
What happens when patients try to book? What have you tried? When would you want it fixed?
A reply to my written offer, then a 50% e-transfer deposit.
One follow-up after 5 days and one after 2 weeks, then I stop.
